newsitem.title: FRANCE: African Franc zone currency to keep value.
newsitem.headline: African Franc zone currency to keep value.

text.p: France assured the 14 members of the African Franc zone on Thursday their French-backed currency would keep its value when the French franc was replaced in 1999 by the planned new European currency to be known as the Euro.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said after hosting a one-day meeting attended by finance ministers from France's former African colonies that there would be no devaluation of the CFA franc currency when European monetary union went into effect.
All that would change when the new European currency was introduced was that the CFA franc's parity would be fixed against the Euro instead of the franc, he said.
The new single European currency is to come into effect under monetary union due to start on January 1, 1999.

The African ministers gave an upbeat message at their regular half-yearly meeting about their countries' economic prospects after the devaluation three years ago of the CFA franc against the French franc.
"The message is one of confidence," Arthuis told reporters.
Thirteen of the African countries devalued their common currency by 50 percent in 1994 and the 14th, the Comoros Islands in the Indian Ocean, devalued by 33 percent.
France precipitated the devaluation by making its aid contingent on the countries winning the International Monetary Fund's backing.
The IMF demanded that they must break a 46-year-old fixed parity with the franc because it made their manufacturing costs higher than their neighbours and was paralysing economic growth.
Since devaluation, growth has returned and exports have climbed. "We have mastered inflation...We have mastered spending," Cote d'Ivoire Finance Minister Niamien N'Goran said.

He said inflation in West Africa had been brought down to between minus one percent and plus nine percent, depending on the country. It had been running at an average 40 percent in the Franc zone only three years ago.

The ministers said growth in the zone should be at least 4.6 percent in 1996 after shrinking on average by 0.8 percent a year from 1990 to 1993. But the ministers said more needed to be done to encourage private investment.

The ministers also urged more progress on debt relief. But N'Goran said he was optimistic the Paris Club of creditor nations would agree to offer better debt relief conditions than the Naples terms currently available -- under which two-thirds of the debt of low-income countries can be written off.

N'Goran said the countries were pressing for the terms to be amended to allow up to 80 percent of the debt to be written off. Debt costs were "preventing essential investment in basic areas like health and education," he said.
Arthuis said France supported easier debt relief on a case by case basis and was optimistic an accord would soon be reached.
